newsitem.title: USA: Lebed said to warn about nuke security in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Lebed said to warn about nuke security in Russia.

text.p: Former Russian national security adviser Alexander Lebed was quoted on Thursday as warning that nuclear security in Russia was unsatisfactory, making the country vulnerable to terrorists.

The outspoken Russian politician issued the warning at a meeting in Washington on Thursday with Republican Sen. Richard Lugar of Indiana, who has sponsored U.S. funds to help reduce the Russian nuclear stockpile, Lugar's office said.

Lebed, a retired general who was fired as national security adviser on Oct. 17 amid intense political jostling while President Boris Yeltsin was awaiting heart surgery, is likely to be a leading contender in the next presidential election.
He placed third, behind Yeltsin, in elections last June.
Lugar's office said in a statement that Lebed had called controls over nuclear material in the former Soviet Union "unsatisfactory," making Russia vulnerable at nuclear plants and facilities.
Lebed emphasised that terrorists need to obtain only a small amount of material to carry out a nuclear attack of devastating proportions, the statement said.
"This is precisely the case where any cost is justified," Lebed was quoted as saying. "Through nuclear terrorism and blackmail, a handful of scoundrels can give the world a tremendous headache."
Experts have warned for years of risks from Russia's nuclear stockpiles, but Russian and U.S. officials habitually respond that they regard the controls as adequate.

Lugar and Georgia Democrat Sam Nunn sponsored a law in 1991 that provides American technical aid to Russia to eliminate nuclear warheads made redundant by arms control pacts, and account for and control nuclear material.

In a sign of Lebed's continuing political clout in Washington, he was received on Thursday at the State Department by Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, architect of U.S. Russia policy in recent years.
State Department spokesman Glyn Davies called it "a good long meeting and a good exchange of views" but gave no further details.
Lebed said later the session was "warm and friendly." He told a news conference he had come to the United States to experience democracy first hand.
"I've seen too much of a mockery ... it is better to see it once than hear it a hundred times," he said through an interpreter.

Asked if he thought he were qualified to lead Russia, Lebed cited the rise of other military men such as Generals Dwight Eisenhower and Charles de Gaulle to the presidencies of the United States and France.
"I think my temperament is okay. Training I lack, so I have decided I must learn," he said.
